text: HR sends you a CSV of 500 new hire records that need to land in sys_user, and they tell you the same file comes back updated every single month, with existing employees needing a refresh instead of a duplicate. Let's walk the whole pipeline through, start to finish, the way you'd actually configure it in a real instance.

Step one is the Data Source. HR is handing you a file, not database or API access, so the correct type is File. You attach the CSV, and because this repeats monthly, you plan a Scheduled Import to automate it — though for this very first run, you load it manually to verify everything works correctly first.

Step two: running that load creates a staging table, something like imp_new_hires, with columns matching the CSV's header row exactly — first_name, last_name, work_email, dept_name. All 500 rows land raw, with no validation yet. A blank email in one row still loads as a blank value, clearly visible for you to catch before it becomes a real problem.

Step three is the Transform Map. Source table imp_new_hires, target table sys_user. work_email maps to email, and dept_name maps to department as a reference lookup against the real Department table. The column names don't need to match at all — the map is exactly where that pairing gets declared.

Step four is coalesce on email. It's unique per person and stays stable across every month's file. A match found on email means update the existing sys_user record's name and department fields. No match found means insert a brand new record instead.

Step five: November's file has the same 500 people plus 40 genuinely new hires. The 500 returning rows match by email and simply update in place — no duplicates created. The 40 new rows insert fresh as brand new users. Skip coalesce entirely, and that same run would have created five hundred and forty duplicate records instead.
That's the full pipeline working together: a Data Source, a staging table, a Transform Map, and coalesce doing the upsert logic. Next up, starting Chapter Seven: Building a Report.
